## Rust

```rust
// Four similarity patterns among the managers; a bigger number means more alike.
let kr_nodes_rows: Vec<Vec<f64>> = kr_nodes.lines().skip(1).map(|l| l.split(',').map(|x| x.parse().unwrap()).collect()).collect();
let (kr_age, kr_tenure, kr_level) = (
    |i: usize| kr_nodes_rows[i][1], |i: usize| kr_nodes_rows[i][2], |i: usize| kr_nodes_rows[i][3],
);
let similarity: Vec<(&str, Dense)> = {
    let build = |f: &dyn Fn(usize, usize) -> f64| {
        let mut m = Dense::zeros(kr_n, kr_n);
        for i in 0..kr_n {
            for j in 0..kr_n {
                m.set(i, j, f(i, j));
            }
        }
        m
    };
    vec![
        ("same department", build(&|i, j| if kr_dept[i] == kr_dept[j] { 1.0 } else { 0.0 })),
        ("same level", build(&|i, j| if kr_level(i) == kr_level(j) { 1.0 } else { 0.0 })),
        ("age closeness", build(&|i, j| -(kr_age(i) - kr_age(j)).abs())),
        ("tenure closeness", build(&|i, j| -(kr_tenure(i) - kr_tenure(j)).abs())),
    ]
};

// Eight QAP tests: two relations by four patterns, 5,000 relabelings each.
let mut family = Vec::new();
for rel in ["advice", "friendship"] {
    let mut y = Dense::zeros(kr_n, kr_n);
    for &(i, j) in &kr_relation(rel) {
        y.set(i, j, 1.0);
    }
    for (label, sim) in &similarity {
        let options = QapCorOptions { mode: QapMode::Digraph, permutations: Permutations::Random { reps: 5_000, seed: 1 }, keep_draws: true, ..Default::default() };
        let test = compute_qap_cor(&y, sim, options)?;
        let hits = test.distribution.iter().filter(|r| r.abs() >= test.statistic.abs() - 1e-12).count();
        family.push((rel, *label, test.statistic, (1 + hits) as f64 / (test.distribution.len() + 1) as f64));
    }
}
// Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg adjustments.
let m = family.len();
let mut order: Vec<usize> = (0..m).collect();
order.sort_by(|&a, &b| family[a].3.partial_cmp(&family[b].3).unwrap());
let (mut holm, mut bh) = (vec![0.0f64; m], vec![0.0f64; m]);
let mut running = 0.0f64;
for (rank, &i) in order.iter().enumerate() {
    running = running.max((m - rank) as f64 * family[i].3);
    holm[i] = running.min(1.0);
}
let mut running = 1.0f64;
for (rank, &i) in order.iter().enumerate().rev() {
    running = running.min(m as f64 / (rank + 1) as f64 * family[i].3);
    bh[i] = running;
}
println!("{:<11} {:<17} {:>6} {:>7} {:>7} {:>7}", "relation", "pattern", "r", "p raw", "p Holm", "p BH");
for &i in &order {
    println!("{:<11} {:<17} {:>6.3} {:>7.4} {:>7.4} {:>7.4}", family[i].0, family[i].1, family[i].2, family[i].3, holm[i], bh[i]);
}
println!(
    "below 0.05: raw {}, Holm {}, BH {}",
    family.iter().filter(|f| f.3 < 0.05).count(), holm.iter().filter(|&&p| p < 0.05).count(), bh.iter().filter(|&&p| p < 0.05).count()
);
```

Four of the eight raw p-values are below 0.05: friendship with department (0.0016), advice with age (0.040) and with tenure (0.041), and friendship with level (0.045). After Holm or Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment only the first survives (0.013 under both), and the other three sit near 0.09 (Benjamini-Hochberg) or 0.28 (Holm). Those three are what you tend to find when you look at eight things. This doesn't prove they are false. It says the evidence for them is no stronger than looking at eight things would produce. It is also the reason to decide what you will test before you look, and to report how many things you tried. The Python tab uses its own relabelings, so its p-values differ in the third decimal.

### Reading a z-score and a percentile

Back to the Florentine families of @sec-small-worlds: 15 families, 20 marriages. Take four statistics and two nulls (random ties, and random networks with the same degrees from stub matching), 2,000 draws each. For each pair we print the observed value, the null's average and spread, the **z-score** (distance from the null's average in standard deviations, @sec-triads-and-motifs), the **percentile** (the share of draws at or below the observed value), the **skewness** of the draws (0 for a symmetric bell, negative for a long tail to the left), and the two-sided p-value.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```r
# The Florentine marriages again (fl_g from the swap block), against two nulls with 2,000 draws each.
fl_degrees <- net_degree(fl_g)
fl_gnm <- net_random_gnm(15, 20, reps = 2000, seed = 1)
fl_cfg <- net_random_config(fl_degrees, simple = TRUE, max_tries = 100000, reps = 2000, seed = 1)
fl_stats <- list(
  transitivity = \(h) as.numeric(net_transitivity(h)),
  `degree assortativity` = \(h) as.numeric(net_assort_degree(h)),
  `mean distance` = \(h) as.numeric(net_mean_distance(h)),
  `largest component` = \(h) max(net_components(h)$csize)
)

# Observed value, the null's average and spread, z-score, percentile, skewness and a two-sided p-value.
compare_to_null <- \(draws, stat, seen) {
  v <- map_dbl(draws, stat)
  tibble(
    observed = seen, null_mean = mean(v), null_sd = sd(v),
    z = (seen - mean(v)) / sd(v),
    percentile = mean(v <= seen + 1e-12),
    skew = mean(((v - mean(v)) / sd(v))^3),
    p_two_sided = (1 + sum(abs(v - mean(v)) >= abs(seen - mean(v)) - 1e-12)) / (length(v) + 1)
  )
}
fl_stats |>
  imap(\(stat, label) {
    list(`random ties` = fl_gnm, `same degrees` = fl_cfg) |>
      imap(\(draws, null_label) {
        compare_to_null(draws, stat, stat(fl_g)) |> mutate(statistic = label, null = null_label, .before = 1)
      }) |>
      list_rbind()
  }) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))

# Suppose the largest component had been 12 families. The z-score and the draws tell different stories.
lc <- map_dbl(fl_cfg, fl_stats[["largest component"]])
z12 <- (12 - mean(lc)) / sd(lc)
tibble(z = z12, share_of_draws_at_most_12 = (1 + sum(lc <= 12)) / (length(lc) + 1)) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), \(x) round(x, 4)))
```

```python
    "degree assortativity": nx.degree_assortativity_coefficient,
    "mean distance": mean_distance,
    "largest component": lambda h: max(len(c) for c in nx.connected_components(h)),
}
print(f"{'statistic':<21} {'null':<13} {'observed':>8} {'null mean':>9} {'null sd':>7} {'z':>6} {'percentile':>10} {'skew':>6} {'p two-sided':>11}")
for label, stat in fl_stats.items():
    seen = stat(fl)
    for null_label, draws in (("random ties", fl_gnm), ("same degrees", fl_cfg)):
        v = np.array([stat(h) for h in draws])
        m, s = v.mean(), v.std(ddof=1)
        two = (1 + np.sum(np.abs(v - m) >= abs(seen - m) - 1e-12)) / (len(v) + 1)
        print(f"{label:<21} {null_label:<13} {seen:>8.3f} {m:>9.3f} {s:>7.3f} {(seen - m) / s:>6.2f} "
              f"{np.mean(v <= seen + 1e-12):>10.3f} {np.mean(((v - m) / s) ** 3):>6.2f} {two:>11.3f}")

# Suppose the largest component had been 12 families. The z-score and the draws tell different stories.
lc = np.array([fl_stats["largest component"](h) for h in fl_cfg])
z12 = (12 - lc.mean()) / lc.std(ddof=1)
print(f"z {z12:.4f}, share of draws at most 12 {(1 + np.sum(lc <= 12)) / (len(lc) + 1):.4f}")
```

```rust
// The Florentine marriages again (fl_graph from the swap block), against two nulls with 2,000 draws each.
let fl_to_graph = |d: &knappnet::generate::EdgeList| {
    let from: Vec<i64> = d.from.iter().map(|&x| x as i64).collect();
    let to: Vec<i64> = d.to.iter().map(|&x| x as i64).collect();
    Graph::from_edges(15, &from, &to, None, false)
};

    .iter().map(|d| fl_to_graph(d).unwrap()).collect();

    .iter().map(|d| fl_to_graph(d).unwrap()).collect();
let fl_stats: Vec<(&str, Box<dyn Fn(&Graph) -> f64>)> = vec![
    ("transitivity", Box::new(|h: &Graph| compute_transitivity(h, ClusteringOptions::default()))),
    ("degree assortativity", Box::new(|h: &Graph| compute_assortativity_degree(h, false, AssortOptions::default()).unwrap())),
    ("mean distance", Box::new(|h: &Graph| compute_mean_distance(h, PathOptions::default(), true).unwrap())),
    ("largest component", Box::new(|h: &Graph| *find_components(h, ComponentKind::Weak).sizes.iter().max().unwrap() as f64)),
];
println!("{:<21} {:<13} {:>8} {:>9} {:>7} {:>6} {:>10} {:>6} {:>11}", "statistic", "null", "observed", "null mean", "null sd", "z", "percentile", "skew", "p two-sided");

    for (null_label, draws) in [("random ties", &fl_gnm), ("same degrees", &fl_cfg)] {
        let v: Vec<f64> = draws.iter().map(|h| stat(h)).collect();
        let (m, s) = mean_sd(&v);
        let two = (1 + v.iter().filter(|&&x| (x - m).abs() >= (seen - m).abs() - 1e-12).count()) as f64 / (v.len() + 1) as f64;
        let below = v.iter().filter(|&&x| x <= seen + 1e-12).count() as f64 / v.len() as f64;
        let skew = v.iter().map(|x| ((x - m) / s).powi(3)).sum::<f64>() / v.len() as f64;
        println!("{:<21} {:<13} {:>8.3} {:>9.3} {:>7.3} {:>6.2} {:>10.3} {:>6.2} {:>11.3}", label, null_label, seen, m, s, (seen - m) / s, below, skew, two);
    }
}

// Suppose the largest component had been 12 families. The z-score and the draws tell different stories.

let z12 = (12.0 - lc_mean) / lc_sd;
println!(
    "z {:.4}, share of draws at most 12 {:.4}",
    z12, (1 + lc.iter().filter(|&&x| x <= 12.0).count()) as f64 / (lc.len() + 1) as f64
);
```

:::

:::

Nothing here is surprising, and that is the finding. No two-sided p-value is below 0.23. Transitivity (0.191) is in the middle of both nulls. Degree assortativity of $-0.375$ (families with many marriages marry families with few) is 1.1 to 1.2 standard deviations below the null's average, percentile 0.13: in the direction of a hub-and-spokes pattern, but well within what 15 families and 20 marriages produce by chance. A small network gives a wide null, so only large effects show. The honest summary is "no evidence against these nulls", not "no pattern": with 20 ties this test has little power.

The z-score and the percentile agree when the null is roughly bell-shaped, as for assortativity (skewness between $-0.05$ and 0.14). They stop agreeing when it isn't. Look at the largest component under the same-degree null: the skewness is $-2.81$, because most draws are connected (15 families) and a few break off a small piece. Suppose the largest component had been 12 families. Its z-score would be $-3.64$, which a normal curve would call rarer than one in a thousand. But 1.5 percent of the draws (0.0150) are at most 12, about one in 67. A z-score assumes a bell shape; the draws don't have one. So read the percentile or the p-value from the draws, show z only for scale, and look at the skewness (or a histogram) whenever the null is lopsided or takes few distinct values. The latter explains the two-sided p-value of 1.000 for transitivity under same degrees: with the degrees fixed, the number of connected triples is fixed, so transitivity moves only in steps of one triangle (about 0.06), and the observed value sits among the middle steps.

## Three ways a null goes wrong

**Too weak.** A null that ignores something obvious in the data makes ordinary patterns look remarkable. In @sec-small-worlds the karate club's transitivity of 0.256 looks nearly twice as clustered as random ties (0.135), but against networks with the same degrees the average is 0.225 and 13 percent of draws are at least as clustered. Reporting only the easy comparison is a quiet way of overselling.

**Too strong.** A null that holds fixed the thing you are studying cannot find it. If your question is whether a few managers attract most of the advice, a null that fixes every manager's number of advice-seekers has answered it before you start. Fixing more is not safer; it changes the question.

**Degenerate.** The worst case is a null that fixes the statistic itself. Take the largest number of marriages any family has (the Medici, with 6), against the two Florentine nulls from above.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```r
# Statistic: the largest number of marriages any one family has (Medici: 6). Reuse the draws from above.
top_degree <- \(draws) map_dbl(draws, \(h) max(net_degree(h)))
list(`random ties` = fl_gnm, `same degrees` = fl_cfg) |>
  imap(\(draws, null_label) {
    top <- top_degree(draws)
    tibble(
      null = null_label, observed = max(fl_degrees), null_mean = mean(top), null_sd = sd(top),
      p_high = (1 + sum(top >= max(fl_degrees))) / (length(top) + 1)
    )
  }) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

Against random ties, a family with 6 marriages is not unusual (average 5.3, upper-tail p-value 0.35). Against the same-degree null, every one of the 2,000 draws has a family with 6 marriages, because the degrees were held fixed: the standard deviation is exactly 0 and the p-value is exactly 1, whatever the network. The test is not saying anything, because the null has already decided. Before running a null, check that your statistic is not a function of what you held fixed. A standard deviation of exactly 0, or a p-value of exactly 1, is the symptom.

## Resampling: the bootstrap, and why the naive one fails

The **bootstrap** [@efron1979bootstrap] has a different job from a permutation test. A permutation test asks whether a pattern is more than a null produces. The bootstrap asks how much an *estimate* would move with different data from the same source: resample the data with replacement, recompute the estimate each time, and read the uncertainty off the spread. For ordinary data it works because the rows are independent units. A network has no such units, and the two obvious ways to resample one both go wrong.

- **Resample people.** Draw $n$ people with replacement and keep the ties among those drawn. A person drawn twice becomes two copies who are not tied to each other, so the resampled network is sparser by construction.
- **Resample ties.** Draw $m$ ties with replacement from the real $m$. A tie drawn twice is still one tie, so each resample keeps only about $1 - 1/e \approx 63$ percent of the distinct ties.

To measure the damage we need a case where the truth is known, so we invent 100 networks of 24 people in which every pair is tied with probability 0.2. The true density is 0.2. For each network we draw 100 resamples of each kind and take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the resampled densities as a 95 percent interval. A method that works would cover 0.2 in about 95 of the 100 networks.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```r
# 100 random networks of 24 people in which every pair is tied with probability 0.2, so the true density
# is 0.2. For each network, 100 bootstrap resamples of each of two kinds.
nb <- 24
nets <- 100
boots <- 100
cap <- 100 # room for up to 100 tie draws per resample
pairs_b <- choose(nb, 2)
pair_ends <- combn(nb, 2)
per_net <- pairs_b + boots * nb + boots * cap
ub <- matrix(stream(99, nets * per_net), nrow = nets, byrow = TRUE)
summarise_boot <- \(values, label, seen) tibble(
  method = label, observed = seen, boot_mean = mean(values), boot_sd = sd(values),
  lo = as.numeric(quantile(values, 0.025)), hi = as.numeric(quantile(values, 0.975))
)
one_network <- \(w) {
  w <- as.vector(w)
  tie <- w[1:pairs_b] < 0.2
  a <- matrix(0, nb, nb)
  a[cbind(pair_ends[1, tie], pair_ends[2, tie])] <- 1
  a <- a + t(a)
  m <- sum(tie)
  # Resample people: draw 24 people with replacement, keep the ties among them (copies of one person are not tied).
  nodes <- matrix(floor(w[(pairs_b + 1):(pairs_b + boots * nb)] * nb) + 1, nrow = boots, byrow = TRUE)
  # Resample ties: draw m of the m ties with replacement; a tie drawn twice is still one tie.
  tie_draws <- matrix(w[(pairs_b + boots * nb + 1):per_net], nrow = boots, byrow = TRUE)[, seq_len(m), drop = FALSE]
  bind_rows(
    summarise_boot(map_dbl(seq_len(boots), \(b) sum(a[nodes[b, ], nodes[b, ]]) / (nb * (nb - 1))),
                   "people resampled", m / pairs_b),
    summarise_boot(map_dbl(seq_len(boots), \(b) length(unique(floor(tie_draws[b, ] * m) + 1)) / pairs_b),
                   "ties resampled", m / pairs_b)
  )
}
asplit(ub, 1) |>
  map(one_network) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  group_by(method) |>
  summarise(
    covers_truth = mean(lo <= 0.2 & 0.2 <= hi),
    average_observed = mean(observed),
    spread_of_observed = sd(observed),
    average_bootstrap_centre = mean(boot_mean),
    average_bootstrap_sd = mean(boot_sd)
  ) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```


## Python

```python
# 100 random networks of 24 people in which every pair is tied with probability 0.2, so the true density
# is 0.2. For each network, 100 bootstrap resamples of each of two kinds.
nb, nets, boots, cap = 24, 100, 100, 100  # cap: room for up to 100 tie draws per resample
pairs_b = nb * (nb - 1) // 2
per_net = pairs_b + boots * nb + boots * cap
ub = stream(99, nets * per_net).reshape(nets, per_net)
pair_i, pair_j = np.triu_indices(nb, 1)

rows = {"people resampled": [], "ties resampled": []}
for w in ub:
    tie = w[:pairs_b] < 0.2
    a = np.zeros((nb, nb))
    a[pair_i[tie], pair_j[tie]] = 1
    a = a + a.T
    m = int(tie.sum())
    # Resample people: draw 24 people with replacement, keep the ties among them (copies of one person are not tied).
    nodes = np.floor(w[pairs_b:pairs_b + boots * nb].reshape(boots, nb) * nb).astype(int)
    # Resample ties: draw m of the m ties with replacement; a tie drawn twice is still one tie.
    tie_draws = w[pairs_b + boots * nb:].reshape(boots, cap)[:, :m]
    for label, values in (
        ("people resampled", [a[np.ix_(i, i)].sum() / (nb * (nb - 1)) for i in nodes]),
        ("ties resampled", [len(set(np.floor(d * m).astype(int))) / pairs_b for d in tie_draws]),
    ):
        lo, hi = np.quantile(values, [0.025, 0.975])
        rows[label].append((m / pairs_b, np.mean(values), np.std(values, ddof=1), lo, hi))

print(f"{'method':<17} {'covers truth':>12} {'avg observed':>12} {'spread of obs.':>14} {'avg boot centre':>15} {'avg boot sd':>11}")
for label, found in rows.items():
    seen, centre, spread, lo, hi = np.array(found).T
    print(f"{label:<17} {np.mean((lo <= 0.2) & (0.2 <= hi)):>12.3f} {seen.mean():>12.3f} {seen.std(ddof=1):>14.3f} "
          f"{centre.mean():>15.3f} {spread.mean():>11.3f}")
```

## Rust

```rust
// 100 random networks of 24 people in which every pair is tied with probability 0.2, so the true density
// is 0.2. For each network, 100 bootstrap resamples of each of two kinds.
let (nb, nets, boots, cap) = (24usize, 100usize, 100usize, 100usize); // cap: room for 100 tie draws per resample
let pairs_b = nb * (nb - 1) / 2;
let per_net = pairs_b + boots * nb + boots * cap;
let ub = pm_stream(99, nets * per_net);
let pair_list: Vec<(usize, usize)> = (0..nb).flat_map(|i| (i + 1..nb).map(move |j| (i, j))).collect();
// Percentile with linear interpolation (what R and NumPy call type 7).
let quantile = |sorted: &[f64], q: f64| -> f64 {
    let pos = q * (sorted.len() - 1) as f64;
    let (lo, hi) = (pos.floor() as usize, pos.ceil() as usize);
    sorted[lo] + (sorted[hi] - sorted[lo]) * (pos - lo as f64)
};
let mut rows: Vec<Vec<[f64; 5]>> = vec![Vec::new(); 2];
for w in ub.chunks(per_net) {
    let mut a = vec![0.0; nb * nb];
    let mut m = 0usize;
    for (k, &(i, j)) in pair_list.iter().enumerate() {
        if w[k] < 0.2 {
            a[i * nb + j] = 1.0;
            a[j * nb + i] = 1.0;
            m += 1;
        }
    }
    let (mut by_people, mut by_ties) = (Vec::new(), Vec::new());
    for b in 0..boots {
        // Resample people: draw 24 people with replacement, keep the ties among them (copies of one person are not tied).
        let people: Vec<usize> = w[pairs_b + b * nb..pairs_b + (b + 1) * nb].iter().map(|x| (x * nb as f64).floor() as usize).collect();
        let kept: f64 = people.iter().map(|&p| people.iter().map(|&q| a[p * nb + q]).sum::<f64>()).sum();
        by_people.push(kept / (nb * (nb - 1)) as f64);
        // Resample ties: draw m of the m ties with replacement; a tie drawn twice is still one tie.
        let start = pairs_b + boots * nb + b * cap;
        let distinct: std::collections::HashSet<usize> = w[start..start + m].iter().map(|x| (x * m as f64).floor() as usize).collect();
        by_ties.push(distinct.len() as f64 / pairs_b as f64);
    }
    for (k, mut values) in [by_people, by_ties].into_iter().enumerate() {
        let (centre, spread) = mean_sd(&values);
        values.sort_by(|x, y| x.partial_cmp(y).unwrap());
        rows[k].push([m as f64 / pairs_b as f64, centre, spread, quantile(&values, 0.025), quantile(&values, 0.975)]);
    }
}
println!("{:<17} {:>12} {:>12} {:>14} {:>15} {:>11}", "method", "covers truth", "avg observed", "spread of obs.", "avg boot centre", "avg boot sd");
for (label, found) in ["people resampled", "ties resampled"].iter().zip(&rows) {
    let column = |c: usize| found.iter().map(|r| r[c]).collect::<Vec<f64>>();
    let covers = found.iter().filter(|r| r[3] <= 0.2 && 0.2 <= r[4]).count() as f64 / nets as f64;
    let (seen_mean, seen_sd) = mean_sd(&column(0));
    println!("{:<17} {:>12.3} {:>12.3} {:>14.3} {:>15.3} {:>11.3}", label, covers, seen_mean, seen_sd, mean_sd(&column(1)).0, mean_sd(&column(2)).0);
}
```

::: {.code-output}
```text
method            covers truth avg observed spread of obs. avg boot centre avg boot sd
people resampled         1.000        0.203          0.022           0.195       0.039
ties resampled           0.010        0.203          0.022           0.129       0.008
```
:::

:::

Resampling ties collapses: the resampled density averages 0.129 against an observed 0.203 (the 63 percent in action), the bootstrap standard deviation is only 0.008, and the intervals contain the truth in 1 network of 100. Resampling people is off in a different way. Its centre is a little low (0.195, from the copies that are never tied) and its spread is far too large: the average bootstrap standard deviation is 0.039, against a real spread of 0.022 in the observed densities across networks. It "covers" the truth in all 100 networks, but only by being 1.8 times too wide. The reason is that resampling people re-draws their *degrees*, and degrees vary more than a pair-by-pair coin flip does. In a network with a different structure the same method could come out too narrow. Its width is not a property of how the data were collected, so it cannot be trusted in either direction.

What to do instead depends on the question. If you want to know whether a pattern is more than a baseline gives, use a null model, as above. If you want uncertainty for the parameters of a model, simulate networks from the fitted model and refit (a parametric bootstrap; see @sec-ergm). And if you really did sample people at random from a population, as in the egocentric designs of @sec-ego-networks, resampling the sampled people's own summaries can be legitimate; the failure here is using the bootstrap for whole-network structure.

## A cheat sheet

| Tool | Question | What it holds fixed | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| QAP correlation | Are two networks (or a network and an attribute pattern) related? | Each matrix's own structure | A relationship is not a cause |
| MRQAP | Is each predictor related to the ties once the others are accounted for? | The same, with several predictors | Overlapping predictors; the default method handles this |
| Random graph with the same number of ties | Is a feature more than size and density alone would give? | Number of people and ties | An easy standard to beat |
| Configuration model | Is a feature more than each person's degree would give? | Everyone's number of ties | Rejection sampling can fail on awkward degree sequences |
| Same degrees by swapping ties | The same, always on simple networks | Everyone's number of ties | Needs enough swaps; knappnet's swap is undirected only |
| Label permutation | Does an attribute line up with the structure? | The network and the group sizes | Says nothing about how the network arose |
| Holm or Benjamini-Hochberg | Several things were tested | Adjusts p-values for how many | Decide the tests before looking |
| Bootstrap by people or ties | How much would my estimate move? | The resampled people or ties | Biased and badly calibrated for network structure |

## Reading tests honestly

**A p-value answers one narrow question.** It says how often chance, *as you defined it*, would produce a result this large. Change the definition of chance and the answer changes. Always say what was held fixed.

**Small networks give lumpy answers.** With ten people, a QAP reference distribution takes only a few distinct values, as @fig-qap-null shows. That is a fact about small data, not a bug. In a network this size you can even list every relabeling exactly, as the exhaustive option does.

**A significant result is not an explanation.** Friends share floors. Maybe people on one floor meet more often, maybe friends pick desks near each other, maybe the company hires through friends. The test can't tell these apart. For explanations that unfold over time, you need data over time (@sec-dynamics).

**Don't hunt.** Test many things and some will pass. Decide what you will test before you look, and say how many things you tried.

**Random draws vary.** Fix the seed, report how many draws you used, and don't read meaning into the last digit. When the stakes are high, run again with more draws. The Monte Carlo error is $\sqrt{p(1-p)/B}$, and a p-value from draws is $(1 + \text{hits})/(B + 1)$, never zero.

**Report the effect, not just the p-value.** A p-value mixes the size of the pattern with the size of the data. Give the share, the correlation or the difference as well.

**Say how many things you tried.** Eight tests at the 5 percent level will pass one by luck about a third of the time. Adjust, or report the count.

**A z-score needs a bell.** When a null is lopsided or takes few values, read the percentile or the p-value from the draws.

**Check that the null doesn't fix your statistic.** A null whose draws all agree on the statistic cannot test it.

**Pick the null that matches the question.** If your claim is "more clustering than a network with these degrees," use the configuration model. If your claim is "more than a random network of this size," the simpler one is the honest comparison. Reporting the easy one when you meant the hard one is a quiet way of overselling.

## Saying it carefully

For each test there is a sentence that the evidence supports and a nearby one that goes further than it can. Every defensible sentence names the network, the statistic, the null (what was held fixed), the number of draws and the size of the effect.

| Test | A defensible sentence | An over-claiming one |
| --- | --- | --- |
| QAP correlation | "Across the 45 pairs, friendship and sharing a floor correlate at 0.365. Of all 3,628,800 relabelings of the ten people, 2.4 percent do at least as well. The two patterns line up in this network." | "Sharing a floor makes people friends (p = 0.02)." |
| MRQAP coefficient | "Holding the (invented) book club fixed, pairs on the same floor are about 0.34 more likely to be friends (permutation p = 0.006, 5,000 relabelings)." | "Floors explain 19 percent of friendship." (The $R^2$ of 0.194 belongs to both predictors together, and describes this network.) |
| Random ties, same count | "In Krackhardt's firm 37 percent of friendship ties stay inside a department against 22 percent expected, and none of 2,000 random networks with 102 ties reaches that (p below 0.001)." | "Friendship in the firm is organized by department." (Most friendship ties, 63 percent, cross departments.) |
| Same degrees | "Transitivity of the Florentine marriages (0.191) is unremarkable among 2,000 random networks with the same degrees (percentile 0.79)." | "The marriage network has no clustering structure." (Fifteen families and 20 marriages give a test with little power.) |
| Many tests | "Of eight pattern-by-relation tests, one (friendship and department) stays below 0.05 after a Holm adjustment (0.013)." | "Advice follows age and tenure (p = 0.04)." (Two of eight raw values near the threshold.) |
| Bootstrap | "Resampling people or ties gave intervals that, in simulation, were far too wide or far too narrow, so we report no bootstrap interval for network-level statistics." | "The 95 percent bootstrap interval for the density is narrow, so the density is estimated precisely." |

## Where this leads

The ideas of this chapter come back with more machinery. @sec-network-regression fits regressions with several predictors, where QAP's relabeling supplies the p-values, and gives the matrix-against-matrix version of the false-alarm experiment. @sec-ergm turns the null model into a statistical model: instead of drawing networks that share your degrees, it draws networks from a distribution with parameters you estimate, and then checks the fit by comparing the observed network with simulated ones, which is the same logic as the percentile above. Earlier chapters already use the tools you met here: @sec-triads-and-motifs compares the triad census with a ladder of nulls, @sec-small-worlds builds configuration and swap baselines, and @sec-homophily shuffles group labels on the karate club. This chapter adds what they leave out: what a p-value from draws is worth, how many things you tried, and what to do when the null is lopsided or degenerate.

## Exercises

1. **By hand.** Two friendship matrices on four people are the same up to relabeling. What does QAP say about their correlation when you try every relabeling? Why does it make sense that a matrix and its relabeled copy can correlate perfectly even though the people are different?
2. **By hand.** In the output above, 21.8 of every 1,000 relabelings reached the observed correlation. If you had asked for 1,000 relabelings instead of 10,000, roughly how much would the share wobble from run to run? (A rough answer is fine: think about how many relabelings landed in the tail.)
3. **Design.** You have a network of who advises whom in a hospital and a table of each person's profession. Which would you test with QAP, and which with a null model? What would you hold fixed in each?
4. **Coding.** Change the seed in the QAP block and rerun it. How much does the p-value move? Then try the exhaustive option (every relabeling, only possible up to ten people) and compare.
5. **Interpretation.** A report says "the network is significantly clustered (p < 0.05)." Write the questions you'd ask the author before believing it.

6. **By hand.** Eight people are split into two floors of four. How many ways are there to choose floor A? What is the smallest p-value an exact label-permutation test can return, if the mirror image (floors swapped) always counts? What changes if the floors have three and five people?
7. **By hand.** A p-value near 0.05 is estimated from 1,000 draws. About how far can it move from run to run? How many draws would you want for an error of 0.002?
8. **By hand.** Five tests give p-values 0.001, 0.012, 0.030, 0.040 and 0.200. Compute the Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted values. How many are below 0.05 under each?
9. **Coding.** Krackhardt's data also hold the formal reporting relation (`reports_to`, 20 ties). Run the relabeling test of department against it. What share of the ties stay inside a department, and what do the ones that leave have in common?
10. **Interpretation.** A paper reports that a network's transitivity is 8 standard deviations above the average of 1,000 random networks with the same number of ties, and concludes that it is "strongly clustered, a small world". Write the questions you would ask before agreeing, and say what you would run to answer them.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Worked answers

1. At least one relabeling lines the two matrices up exactly, so the relabeling distribution contains the value 1, the largest correlation possible. If the matrices as given are aligned, the observed correlation is 1, and the exact p-value is the number of relabelings that reach 1, divided by 24, so at least 1/24. If they are not aligned, the observed correlation is lower and the p-value is larger. A correlation of two 0-1 matrices only asks whether the *same pairs* are tied in both; the names of the people don't enter, which is why a matrix and a relabeled copy of itself can match perfectly.
2. With about 22 relabelings in the tail of 1,000, the count wobbles by about $\sqrt{22} \approx 4.7$, so the share by about 0.005, or roughly 20 to 25 in 1,000. The formula gives $\sqrt{0.0218 \times 0.9782 / 1000} = 0.0046$. The chapter's exact share, 0.0238, sits inside that range.
3. Use QAP (or, equivalently, a label permutation) for "do people tend to advise within their own profession?": build a same-profession matrix, keep the advice network and that matrix as they are, and relabel people. Use a null model for a question about the advice network alone, such as "is there more reciprocity than networks with the same number of ties, or the same in- and out-degrees, would give?". In each case say what is held fixed.
4. At 10,000 relabelings the p-value should move by about 0.0015 between seeds (the chapter's table), so the third decimal is noise. The exhaustive version gives 0.0238 for the chapter's friendship and floor data.
5. Ask: clustering by which measure (global or average local)? Compared with what (random ties, same degrees, something else), how many draws, which seed? Was this one test of many? Is the network complete or a sample, and who is missing? How big is the effect (the clustering itself, not only the p-value)? Would the conclusion survive dropping a tenth of the ties?
6. There are $\binom{8}{4} = 70$ ways to choose floor A. The real split and its mirror image always reach the observed count, so the smallest p-value is $2/70 = 0.029$. With floors of three and five there is no mirror image (swapping the labels would make floors of five and three), so each of the $\binom{8}{3} = 56$ splits counts once and the smallest p-value is $1/56 = 0.018$.
7. The standard deviation is $\sqrt{0.05 \times 0.95 / 1000} = 0.0069$, so about plus or minus 0.007 (a p-value of 0.05 could come back as 0.04 or 0.06). For an error of 0.002 you need $0.05 \times 0.95 / 0.002^2 \approx 11{,}900$ draws.
8. Holm: $5 \times 0.001 = 0.005$; $4 \times 0.012 = 0.048$; $3 \times 0.030 = 0.09$; $2 \times 0.040 = 0.08$, raised to 0.09 so the values never decrease; $1 \times 0.200 = 0.2$. Two are below 0.05 (0.005 and 0.048). Benjamini-Hochberg: $p \times 5 / \text{rank}$ gives 0.005, 0.030, 0.050, 0.050, 0.200, and taking the running minimum from the largest down leaves them the same. Two are below 0.05 (0.005 and 0.030); the two at 0.050 are not below it.
9. Of the 20 reporting ties, 16 (80 percent) stay inside a department, against about 22 percent expected, and the relabeling p-value is the smallest 5,000 draws allow, about 0.0002. The four ties that leave a department all go to the CEO, who is alone in department 0. The test is "significant" and also nearly empty of information: the reporting structure is the organization chart that defines departments.
10. Ask which random networks: the same number of ties only, or the same degrees as well? In @sec-small-worlds the karate club looks nearly twice as clustered as random ties give (0.256 against 0.135) but only a little above networks with its degrees (0.225, with 13 percent of draws at least as clustered). Ask for the percentile and the number of draws, not only z, because a z-score of 8 from a lopsided null means little; ask how big the difference is in transitivity itself; and note that "small world" also needs short distances, which a transitivity z-score says nothing about. To answer, rerun with degree-preserving swaps, report percentiles and the number of draws, and give the clustering and the distances themselves.
:::

## Summary

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
Ordinary tests treat each pair of people as an independent observation, which network data can't be, because pairs that share a person are bundled together. QAP keeps the bundling by relabeling people in one matrix and recomputing the correlation, and MRQAP does the same with several predictors. Null models do the job for a single network by drawing random networks that share some features with yours: the same size and number of ties, or the same degrees as well. The friendship network leans toward same-floor friendships (correlation 0.365, a QAP share of 0.022) and is more clustered than random networks with the same size or the same degrees. All of these p-values depend on what chance means, so say what you held fixed. A p-value from random draws is itself an estimate with a Monte Carlo error you can compute, and it is never exactly zero. Report it with an effect size and with the number of things you tried, and read a z-score only when the null is bell-shaped. Some nulls fix the statistic they are asked to test, and the naive bootstrap, which resamples people or ties, is biased for networks. Say what the evidence supports and no more.
:::

## Further reading

For the origin of QAP, see @hubert1976quadratic and @hubert1987assignment, and for its use with network data, @krackhardt1987qap and @krackhardt1988predicting. For why the double semi-partialling default is safe with overlapping predictors, see @dekker2007sensitivity. For random graph models, see @erdos1959random and @gilbert1959random, and for the configuration model, @molloy1995critical and @newman2001random. For degree-preserving rewiring, see @maslov2002specificity. For a textbook treatment of testing with network data, see @hanneman2005introduction. For why permutation p-values should never be zero, see @phipson2010permutation, for tie swapping as a sampler, @fosdick2018configuring, and for the bootstrap, @efron1979bootstrap. For multiple testing, see @holm1979simple and @benjamini1995controlling. For a statistical treatment of network summaries, see @kolaczyk2009statistical and @wasserman1994social. To practice in R, Phil Murphy's tutorials on hypothesis testing [@murphyrpubs338798], QAP [@murphyrpubs539996; @murphyrpubs679837] and conditional uniform graphs [@murphyrpubs536741] are good companions.
